items.title: What Emotional Intelligence Is — Concept & Origins
items.body:
## Definition

**Emotional Intelligence (EI/EQ)** is the ability to **recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions**, and to **perceive and respond effectively to the emotions of others**. It is not about suppressing emotion, but about using emotional information intelligently.

## Origins

- **Peter Salovey & John Mayer (1990)** coined the term 'emotional intelligence'.
- **Daniel Goleman (1995)** popularised it in his bestseller *Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ*.
- **Reuven Bar-On** developed the mixed 'EQ-i' model and popularised the term **EQ** (Emotional Quotient).

## EI vs IQ

| Trait | IQ | EI |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | Cognitive / analytical ability | Emotional & social ability |
| Stability | Relatively fixed | **Can be learned & developed** |
| Role in leadership | A threshold requirement | A key differentiator of success |

Goleman's central argument: for leadership and life success, **EI can matter more than IQ**.
keyPoints: EI = recognising, understanding and managing one's own emotions and responding effectively to others' emotions.
Salovey & Mayer coined 'emotional intelligence' in 1990; Goleman popularised it in his 1995 book.
Bar-On developed the EQ-i mixed model and popularised the term 'EQ' (Emotional Quotient).
IQ is relatively stable and cognitive; EI is developable and emotional/social.
Goleman argued EI can matter more than IQ for effective leadership.
items.source: Salovey & Mayer (1990); Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); Britannica — Emotional Intelligence

items.title: Goleman's Five Components of EI
items.body:
## The five components

Goleman groups EI into **five components** — the first three are *personal* (managing yourself) and the last two are *social* (managing relationships).

| # | Component | Meaning | Scenario cue |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Self-awareness** | Recognise your own emotions, triggers and their impact | "I notice I'm getting angry" |
| 2 | **Self-regulation** | Control impulsive feelings; think before acting; self-discipline | Pausing before reacting |
| 3 | **Motivation** | Inner drive to achieve; optimism; resilience after setbacks | Persisting after failure |
| 4 | **Empathy** | Understand and share others' feelings without judgment | Reading a colleague's mood |
| 5 | **Social skills** | Build rapport, communicate, manage conflict and relationships | Mediating a team dispute |

## Order matters

- **Self-awareness precedes self-regulation** — you must notice a feeling before you can manage it.
- The personal competencies (1–3) are the base on which the social competencies (4–5) are built.
keyPoints: Goleman's five EI components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
Personal competencies = self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation; social competencies = empathy, social skills.
Self-awareness = recognising one's own emotions and triggers; it is the foundational competency.
Self-regulation = controlling impulses and thinking before acting.
Empathy = sensing others' feelings; social skills = managing relationships and resolving conflict.
items.mnemonic: Personal-then-social: 'SSM-ES' = Self-awareness, Self-regulation, Motivation (self) → Empathy, Social skills (others).
items.source: Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995) & Working with Emotional Intelligence (1998)

items.title: The Mayer-Salovey Four-Branch Ability Model
items.body:
## Four branches (basic → complex)

Unlike Goleman's 'mixed' model, Mayer & Salovey treat EI as a set of **abilities**, ordered from most basic to most complex:

| Branch | Ability | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 **Perceiving** emotions | Detect emotions in faces, voices, oneself | Reading a frown as displeasure |
| 2 **Using / facilitating** emotions | Harness emotions to aid thinking & problem-solving | Using enthusiasm to brainstorm |
| 3 **Understanding** emotions | Grasp emotional meanings, blends and transitions | Knowing anxiety can turn to relief |
| 4 **Managing** emotions | Regulate emotions in self and others | Calming a tense meeting |

## Key contrast

- **Ability model (Mayer-Salovey):** EI is a mental aptitude, measured by performance tests (e.g. MSCEIT).
- **Mixed model (Goleman / Bar-On):** EI blends abilities with personality traits and competencies.
keyPoints: Mayer-Salovey four-branch model orders abilities: Perceiving → Using → Understanding → Managing emotions.
Perceiving emotions is the most basic branch; managing emotions is the most complex.
The Mayer-Salovey approach is an 'ability' model, measured by performance tests like the MSCEIT.
Goleman's and Bar-On's approaches are 'mixed' models blending abilities with traits/competencies.
items.source: Mayer, Salovey & Caruso — four-branch ability model

items.title: Cracking EI Scenario Questions (Administrator Dilemmas)
items.body:
## The method

APPSC EI items give a **situation** and four responses; pick the **emotionally intelligent, defensible best option**. Use this filter:

1. **Eliminate aggressive/impulsive options** — retaliation, threats, shouting, public rebukes (fail self-regulation).
2. **Eliminate passive/avoidant options** — ignoring, doing nothing, brushing off, escaping responsibility (fail ownership).
3. **Eliminate over-reactions** — disproportionate punishment or drastic transfers that dodge the real issue.
4. **Choose the balanced response** — usually: *stay calm → acknowledge the emotion → understand the facts → act fairly toward a solution.*

## The winning template

> **Listen calmly → acknowledge the feeling → analyse/verify → respond constructively.**

This pattern (composure + empathy + responsibility) is almost always the intended answer.

## Common traps

- 'Strong' confident-sounding options that are actually **defensive or ego-driven**.
- 'Kind' options that **remove the person's agency** (e.g. silently reassigning all their work).
- Options that solve the **task** but ignore the **emotion**, or vice-versa — the best answer handles both.
keyPoints: In EI scenarios, eliminate aggressive/impulsive options and passive/avoidant options first.
Winning template: stay calm → acknowledge the emotion → verify facts → respond constructively.
Beware 'confident' options that are really defensive/ego-driven, and 'kind' options that remove a person's agency.
The best answer handles both the task and the emotion, fairly and proportionately.
items.mnemonic: CAVA — Calm, Acknowledge, Verify, Act fairly.
items.source: Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); local APPSC GK PDF — Verbal Reasoning: Emotional Intelligence
